---
title: "The number of ordered grade reports"
subtitle: "2.3 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 14, and the postrank vignette m5"
description: "Sizes of unrestricted, grade-restricted and fixed-order report families."
---

A grade report partitions units into groups and orders those groups. The set of possible reports therefore includes
all strict rankings as well as reports with shared grades. Restrictions on the number of occupied grades, or on the
order in which groups may occur, reduce this set. The curves compare the resulting family sizes on a logarithmic
scale. The small examples identify the groupings and orders counted as distinct reports. These are combinatorial
counts; calculating them does not require evaluating the reporting risk of each candidate.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Three units.** There are 13 ordered grade reports but only 6 strict rankings. In the small examples,
  some reports group letters, while others give each letter its own box. Swapping the positions of occupied boxes
  changes which directions are stated.
- **Six units.** All reports number 4,683. A cap permits 603, while an exact grade count permits 540; cuts of one
  declared order permit only 32. The capped family includes reports with fewer occupied grades, which explains
  its larger count than the exact family.
- **Eight units.** All reports reach 545,835, compared with 6,051 under the cap and 128 along one order. The
  dashed lines identify the families even where their counts are close. Arrow-key selection and the table give the exact count for each unit count and family.
- **Twelve units.** There are 28,091,567,595 reports in the full family, while the cap leaves 523,251. The hollow
  squares mark problem sizes encountered elsewhere in this collection. Counting those possibilities does not
  require generating every report.
- **An empty exact family.** The small example has 0 reports: the requested number of nonempty grades exceeds
  its number of units. An empty family has no logarithmic height, so its count stays visible in the table.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A declared order permits only contiguous cuts of that order, without equal-score blocks here. This is a
substantive restriction on the available reports. Counts describe family size; they say neither which report
has smallest risk nor how long a particular optimisation algorithm will take.
:::

Standalone: [report counts](../../embed/how-many-reports.html), for example `?n=8&G=3`.
